note.specFocus: Christian attitudes to celibacy, contraception and childlessness, including why celibacy is valued in some traditions.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.8 Childlessness and Celibacy
Christian teaching recognises a range of situations around children and sexual relationships, including the deliberate choice of celibacy.
Celibacy
• St Paul, in 1 Corinthians 7:32–35, teaches that an unmarried person can be "anxious about the things of the Lord" without the competing responsibilities of marriage — meaning celibacy is valued as a way to devote oneself fully to God's service.
• In Catholic and Orthodox tradition, priests, monks and nuns are generally required to remain celibate, following what is understood as the model of Jesus' own unmarried life and symbolising total dedication to the Church.
• Most Protestant traditions do not require clerical celibacy, allowing ministers to marry and have families.
Childlessness
• Couples may be childless involuntarily (infertility) or by choice; Christian attitudes to assisted fertility treatment vary, with the Catholic Church generally opposing techniques that involve destroying embryos or separating conception from the marital act, while many Protestant Christians are more accepting of IVF and similar treatments.
• Adoption and fostering are widely encouraged by Christian churches as a loving response to childlessness and a way of caring for children in need of a family.
Contraception
• The Catholic Church teaches that artificial contraception is not permitted, as it separates the unitive and procreative purposes of marriage, though natural family planning is accepted.
• Most Protestant Christians accept contraception as a responsible way for couples to plan their family.
Exam link: do not confuse celibacy (a deliberate vocation, often linked to ministry) with childlessness (which may be involuntary) — questions distinguish clearly between the two.

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. St Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 7:32–35 that an unmarried person can be "anxious about the things of the Lord" without the competing responsibilities of marriage, so celibacy is valued by many Christians as a way of devoting oneself fully to God's work.

2. In the Catholic tradition, priests, monks and nuns are generally required to remain celibate, following what is seen as the example of Jesus himself, who did not marry, and symbolising total dedication to the Church; most Protestant traditions do not require clergy to be celibate.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two beliefs about celibacy.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Some argue that celibacy goes against a basic human need for intimacy and family life, and that most Protestant traditions, which do not require clerical celibacy, show that close devotion to God does not actually require giving up marriage.

A second consideration is: Humanists and other critics may see enforced celibacy, such as in some cases of clerical abuse scandals, as having caused serious harm, arguing this shows celibacy can create more problems than it solves.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Catholic and monastic tradition sees celibacy as a genuine vocation and gift, following 1 Corinthians 7, which frees a person from family responsibilities so they can devote themselves fully and without distraction to prayer, ministry and service to others.

A further consideration is: Celibate figures such as monks, nuns and many priests have historically contributed enormously to education, care for the poor and the sick, and the spiritual life of the Church, which many see as clear evidence that celibacy has served a valuable and far from pointless purpose.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: whether celibacy is judged by whether it suits every individual, or by whether it has value as one legitimate vocation among several ways of serving God. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of vocation, dedicated Church service, human dignity and sensitive pastoral care and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
